title: Record of Lodoss War: Advent of Cardice
subtitle: A warrior brought back to life
summary: Record of Lodoss War: Advent of Cardice is Neverland's action role-playing game, first released for Dreamcast in Japan on 29 June 2000.
body: Record of Lodoss War: Advent of Cardice is Neverland's action role-playing game, first released for Dreamcast in Japan on 29 June 2000. Set in the fantasy world created by Ryō Mizuno, it follows a hero resurrected by the wizard Wart to oppose the destructive goddess Cardice. Fighting enemies and gathering equipment carry the adventure forward, but much of the character's growth depends on a blacksmith. The materials and inscribed plaques found during the journey become a way to shape the hero's strength, connecting exploration directly to the equipment taken into battle.

Experience levels increase the hero's health, while other statistics depend on mithrill inscriptions placed in weapons and armour. A plaque supplies a particular effect, and the blacksmith requires enough mithrill to apply it. The same inscription can be repeated when sufficient material is available, allowing the player to concentrate improvements where they are wanted. Finding another plaque therefore offers a lasting possibility rather than a single temporary item. The system gives gathered resources a clear destination and makes a return to the blacksmith part of preparing for the next expedition.

Discovering a better weapon does not require abandoning all the inscriptions accumulated on the old one. The blacksmith can transform existing equipment to match a newly found example of the same type while retaining its previous improvements. That continuity lets the player welcome a discovery without losing the value of earlier materials. The adventure's equipment becomes a record of the route already travelled, carrying repeated investments into later battles. Within a familiar fantasy setting, this relationship between found objects, permanent inscriptions and reforging gives the character's development its distinctive practical rhythm.
